record.paper_title: Current Unsolved Problems in Planetary Nebulae Research
record.original_question: What definition of a planetary nebula is precise enough to distinguish a true planetary nebula from observational mimics such as emission-line galaxies, reflection nebulae, H II regions, Wolf-Rayet nebulae, novae, supernova remnants, young stellar objects, and symbiotic stars, while still requiring both an ionized circumstellar shell and the correct evolutionary connection to an asymptotic giant branch progenitor and its hot post-AGB or pre-white-dwarf central star?

evidence.quote: The question of "what is a planetary nebula" is not as straightforward as one might think.
Most fundamentally, we need a clear definition of the planetary nebula phenomenon so that our studies are not confused with objects in other stages of stellar evolution.

artifact.status_search_result: No universally accepted, operational definition of a planetary nebula that simultaneously enforces the AGB/post-AGB evolutionary connection and reliably excludes all listed mimic classes is known; the problem remains an open conceptual issue actively discussed in the planetary-nebula community, including in IAU symposia and review articles by Frew & Parker and others.

status_evidence.title: Planetary Nebulae: Observational Properties, Mimics and Diagnostics — Frew & Parker (2010)
status_evidence.snippet: We discuss the difficulties in defining a planetary nebula and present a working definition... numerous classes of mimics including symbiotic stars, H II regions, Wolf–Rayet shells, supernova remnants and others can masquerade as PNe.
status_evidence.claim: A widely cited working definition exists but the authors explicitly note that no fully unambiguous definition has been agreed upon, and mimic discrimination remains problematic.
